flawed_step: Lines 0047-0065 (the (⇐) direction): 'Let C = (v1,...,vk,v1) be a simple cycle in G with k ≥ 2' together with the construction R2 = {(v1,v3),(v3,v4),...,(vk-1,vk),(vk,v2),(v2,v1)} at line 0053 and the claim at line 0058 that R2 is a different Hamiltonian cycle on the cycle vertices, and at lines 0059-0064 that both R1 and R2 are minimum with (R1)T = (R2)T = GT.
counterexample: Take G on two vertices V = {a, b} with edge set E = {a→b, b→a}. G is not acyclic: C = (a, b, a) is a simple cycle of length k = 2. Its transitive closure is GT = {a→b, b→a} (plus the self-loops a→a, b→b if paths of length 2 are counted; the argument below is unaffected either way). Now enumerate candidate reductions. One edge is not enough: any single-edge graph has transitive closure of size at most 1 on {a,b} and cannot contain both a→b and b→a, so no 1-edge graph has closure GT; likewise the empty graph fails. So the minimum is 2 edges, and among the 2-edge subsets of {a→a, a→b, b→a, b→b} only {a→b, b→a} has closure GT: {a→a, b→b} has closure {a→a, b→b}; {a→b, a→a} has no b→a in its closure; {a→b, b→b} has no b→a; symmetrically for the pairs containing only b→a. Hence G has EXACTLY ONE transitive reduction, namely G itself, even though G is cyclic. This refutes the (⇐) direction's conclusion, and it breaks the proof's construction verbatim: for k = 2 the set R2 of line 0053 degenerates to {(v2,v2),(v2,v1)} = {b→b, b→a} — the term (v1,v3) does not exist and (vk,v2) becomes the self-loop (v2,v2) — so R2 is not a Hamiltonian cycle at all and its transitive closure {b→b, b→a} ≠ GT, contradicting line 0060-0063. There is no 'different Hamiltonian cycle' on 2 vertices, so the claimed pair R1 ≠ R2 does not exist for k = 2.
reasoning_summary: The forward direction (acyclic ⇒ unique) is standard and the proof's Lemmas 1-3 are essentially the usual argument. The risky claim is the converse at lines 0046-0065, which asserts that ANY cycle of length k ≥ 2 yields two distinct minimum edge sets by reversing/re-routing the cycle. I tested the smallest allowed case, k = 2, on G = ({a,b}, {a→b, b→a}). The proof's R2 formula is literally malformed there (it references v3, which does not exist, and produces a self-loop (v2,v2)), and more importantly the conclusion is false: an exhaustive check of all edge sets on two vertices shows {a→b, b→a} is the unique minimum-edge graph whose transitive closure equals GT. So a cyclic graph with a unique transitive reduction exists, and the 'only if' direction as proved (and as stated) fails. The gap is not merely cosmetic — a 2-cycle (more generally, a strongly connected component of size 2) genuinely admits only one reduction, so no repair of the R2 formula rescues the argument at k = 2.
